subject: Computing
framework: National Curriculum in England (2014): Computing programmes of study (Key Stages 1 to 3), with an early-years technology foundation for Reception
statusNote: Key stage statements were read and paraphrased from the gov.uk National Curriculum computing programmes of study. The EYFS statutory framework (September 2026 version) has no technology-specific early learning goal, so the Reception year map is a recommended early-skills sequence, not statutory content. Statutory content is set by key stage, not by year; the year allocation is a recommended sequence aligned to the school's existing unit names.

purpose: Computing education builds computational thinking and creativity, with links to mathematics, science, and design and technology.
It rests on three strands: computer science, information technology and digital literacy.
Pupils learn to write programs, solve problems by breaking them into parts, and understand how computers work.
Pupils become responsible, confident and creative users of digital technology.

statements: Follow and give simple step-by-step instructions, in unplugged and floor-robot activities.
Use simple devices with adult guidance to look at, make and save pictures and sounds.
Talk about everyday technology and begin to know how to ask for help.
Understand what algorithms are and that programs follow exact, unambiguous instructions.
Create and debug simple programs.
Use logical reasoning to predict the behaviour of simple programs.
Use technology purposefully to create, organise, store, manipulate and retrieve digital content.
Recognise common uses of information technology beyond school.
Use technology safely and respectfully, keep personal information private, and know where to get help.
Design, write and debug programs for goals, including controlling or simulating physical systems.
Solve problems by decomposing them into smaller parts.
Use sequence, selection, repetition, variables and input and output in programs.
Use logical reasoning to explain algorithms and to detect and correct errors.
Understand computer networks, including the internet, and the services they provide.
Select, use and combine software and online services to create programs, systems and content.
Collect, analyse, evaluate and present data and information.
Use search technologies effectively and understand how results are selected and ranked.
Judge the reliability of digital content and be discerning in evaluating it.
Use technology safely, respectfully and responsibly; recognise unacceptable behaviour and know how to report concerns.
Design, use and evaluate computational abstractions that model real-world problems and systems.
Understand key algorithms, such as sorting and searching, and compare their suitability.
Use two or more programming languages, at least one text-based, to solve problems.
Use data structures such as lists and tables, and modular code with procedures or functions.
Design and develop modular programs and understand how to test and evaluate them.
Understand simple Boolean logic and its use in circuits and programming.
Understand binary numbers and perform simple binary conversions and calculations.
Understand hardware and software, and how instructions are stored and executed.
Understand how text, sounds and pictures are represented as binary data.
Undertake creative projects that combine applications, selecting and using them for known users.
Create, reuse, revise and repurpose digital artefacts for an audience, considering trust, design and usability.
Use technology safely, respectfully, responsibly and securely, protecting online identity and privacy.
Recognise inappropriate content, contact and conduct, and know how to report concerns.

toKS4: Key Stage 3 prepares pupils for Pearson Edexcel GCSE Computer Science 1CP2 (Paper 1 Topics 1 to 5, Paper 2 Topic 6 in Python 3). Algorithms, flowcharts, searching and sorting set up Topic 1 (1.1 to 1.3). Binary, data representation and file sizes set up Topic 2. Hardware, software and translators set up Topic 3. Networks and protocols set up Topic 4. Online safety, ethics, law and the environment set up Topic 5. Scratch then Python, with functions, lists and strings, set up Topic 6 (6.1 to 6.6), which is assessed by an on-screen programming exam.

links.topic: Binary numbers, place value and number bases
links.how: Maths supplies place value and powers; Computing applies them to binary, hexadecimal and file sizes.
Maths develops number patterns and algebra; Computing expresses them as algorithms, loops and functions.

links.topic: Boolean logic, sets and Venn diagrams
links.how: Maths uses AND, OR and NOT in Venn diagrams; Computing uses them in conditions and truth tables.

links.topic: Data handling: averages, charts and spreadsheets
links.how: Maths teaches averages and charts; Computing uses spreadsheets to calculate and present them.
Science collects measurements; Computing writes programs that read sensors and control systems.
Physics studies circuits and switches; Computing models them as logic gates and Boolean expressions.
Design and Technology designs products; Computing programs the control systems inside them.
Geography gathers fieldwork data; Computing uses spreadsheets and online maps to analyse and present it.

links.topic: Writing for an audience and evaluating sources
links.how: English teaches drafting and judging sources; Computing applies them to digital content and online searching.
PSHE teaches respect and wellbeing; Computing teaches privacy, security and how to report online concerns.
Art teaches composition; Computing teaches how digital images and sound are created and stored.

gaps: The EYFS framework has no technology-specific early learning goal; the Reception year map is a recommended sequence and not statutory content.
Year-by-year allocation of units is a recommended sequence aligned to the school's existing unit names; the National Curriculum fixes content by key stage, not by year.

Links to GCSE 1CP2 section numbers come from the Pearson getting started guide and a school-hosted copy of the specification; the Pearson specification PDF itself was not opened (see ks4/computing.json).
Hexadecimal and file-size work in Year 9 is a recommended extension beyond the statutory binary requirement.
